strengths: The paper identifies a practical and relatively underexplored problem: feed-forward generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting in the presence of transient distractors during both training and inference.

The proposed framework is coherent, combining reference-based mask filtering, refinement with segmentation priors, reference re-selection, and 3D Gaussian pruning. The components are well motivated by the failure modes of loss-only robust masking.

Experiments include comparisons to generalizable 3DGS baselines, adapted distractor-free methods, pretrained models, fine-tuning settings, and several ablations. The reported gains over MVSplat and mask-augmented variants are substantial on the tested scenes.
The qualitative figures support the main intuition that naive robust masks can over-mask hard static regions, while the proposed reference-guided procedure better preserves scene content.
weaknesses: The evaluation is not yet fully convincing for a top-tier acceptance. The real-data benchmark appears small, with means over five RobustNeRF scenes and selected On-the-go scenes, and many important details are deferred to an appendix that is not present in the provided manuscript.

Claims about superior mask prediction, including outperforming scene-specific methods, are only supported qualitatively. There are no quantitative mask metrics, no human-labeled mask evaluation, and no uncertainty analysis for distractor versus hard-to-reconstruct static regions.

The comparisons to scene-specific distractor-free methods may be unfair or under-specified, since those methods are adapted into the generalizable training loss rather than run in their native setting. It is unclear whether their hyperparameters, segmentation choices, and optimization budgets were tuned comparably.

The method depends heavily on an external pretrained entity segmentation model and precomputed segmentation masks, weakening the claim of unsupervised/generalizable distractor masking and making the pipeline less self-contained. The computational and failure-mode implications of this dependency are only lightly discussed.

The inference setup assumes access to a nearby scene-image pool around the query and uses reference scoring over that pool. This may be reasonable for video-like captures, but the paper does not clearly analyze how performance changes when the pool is sparse, badly ordered, or dominated by distractors.

Some technical details are ambiguous or confusing, especially the mask notation, union/intersection operations, thresholds, warping/depth handling, and pruning rule. These ambiguities make the method difficult to reproduce.

Reproducibility is limited: code is promised but not available in the manuscript, hyperparameter details are incomplete, synthetic dataset construction is only briefly described, and there is no full training budget or architecture specification beyond relying on MVSplat.
The writing has frequent grammatical issues and some overclaiming, which obscures the exact contribution and the conditions under which the method is expected to work.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically relevant problem: handling transient distractors in feed-forward, generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting rather than only in per-scene optimization settings.
The proposed framework has a coherent high-level decomposition into distractor-aware training, reference-based mask refinement, reference re-selection, and 3D primitive pruning.

The reported quantitative gains over MVSplat and several adapted mask-based baselines on RobustNeRF are sizable, and the ablations suggest that reference-based mask prediction is the main contributor.
The qualitative examples indicate that the method can reduce visible distractor artifacts in some scenes.
weaknesses: The evaluation is too narrow and not fully convincing for a top-tier venue. The main quantitative table is centered on RobustNeRF with only a five-scene mean, while On-the-go and synthetic results are presented only partially or qualitatively in the main paper.

The evaluation protocol raises concerns: at test time the candidate reference pool is constructed from views closest to each query and is explicitly arranged to include both distractor-containing and some distractor-free data. This may make the reference scoring task easier than realistic deployment and weakens the claimed generality.

Several important claims are insufficiently supported, especially the claim that the method predicts masks better than scene-specific methods. The paper provides qualitative mask comparisons but no quantitative mask accuracy, IoU, precision/recall, or human evaluation.

Baselines are not entirely satisfying. Scene-specific distractor-removal methods are adapted by inserting their masks into MVSplat training, but it is unclear whether these adaptations are faithful, tuned, or competitive. Strong recent generalizable reconstruction methods beyond the chosen MVSplat/Pixelsplat backbone receive limited treatment.

The method depends on an external entity segmentation model and cached pre-segmentation, but the computational cost, failure modes, and sensitivity to this model are not adequately analyzed. The efficiency table is especially incomplete because it focuses on rendering time and gives only a bracketed number with pre-segmentation.

Reproducibility is weak in the manuscript: many details are deferred to an appendix that is not present in the provided paper, including synthetic data construction, training details, and additional results. Code is only promised, not available.

The technical presentation is often unclear. Some equations and notation are hard to parse, the mask fusion logic is not rigorously justified, and the distinction between distractor masks and disparity/occlusion masks is not always precise.

The paper overstates novelty and impact. The components are plausible combinations of robust masking, multi-view warping, segmentation priors, reference selection, and pruning, but the conceptual advance beyond adapting existing ideas to generalizable 3DGS is moderate.

Failure cases are underdeveloped. The paper briefly mentions degradation under common occlusions, but does not systematically characterize when reference selection, mask prediction, or pruning harms reconstruction.
Writing and presentation issues, including grammatical errors, crowded figures, small tables, and imprecise claims, make the paper harder to assess and reduce confidence in the experimental rigor.

strengths: The paper identifies a practically important and underexplored setting: feedforward, generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting in the presence of distractors, bridging generalizable reconstruction and distractor-robust scene-specific reconstruction.

The proposed DGGS framework is technically coherent, with complementary training-time mask prediction/refinement and inference-time reference scoring/pruning components that address distinct failure modes.

The empirical gains over MVSplat/Pixelsplat and several adapted distractor-mask baselines are substantial on the reported real-world benchmarks, especially in PSNR and LPIPS, and the ablations support the contribution of the main modules.
The method is appealing because it predicts distractor masks without direct mask supervision and appears to improve both reconstruction quality and mask quality qualitatively.
The paper includes useful component ablations for robust masks, reference-based filtering, mask refinement, auxiliary loss, reference scoring, pruning, and sensitivity to reference/pool size.
weaknesses: The real-world evaluation is still relatively narrow: training and testing are based on a small number of scenes from On-the-go and RobustNeRF, with only five scenes summarized in the main quantitative table. This limits confidence in broad cross-scene generalization.

The evaluation protocol constructs the inference image pool using views closest to the query and ensures inclusion of both distractor-containing and some distractor-free data. This may overstate performance relative to unconstrained deployment, and the practical assumptions about pose availability, pool construction, and distractor-free candidate availability need clearer justification.

Mask quality is mostly shown qualitatively. Since a central claim is superior generalizable distractor masking, quantitative mask evaluation on synthetic data or manually annotated real frames would significantly strengthen the evidence.

The method relies on an external entity segmentation model and several heuristic thresholds/hyperparameters. The robustness of these choices across domains, distractor types, and segmentation failures is not fully established.

Some comparisons adapt scene-specific distractor methods into the generalizable training loss, but it is unclear whether these baselines are optimally tuned for this new setting. This leaves some uncertainty about the fairness and strength of the baseline implementations.

Synthetic experiments are only briefly presented in the main paper and appear mostly qualitative. More quantitative synthetic results, where distractor masks and clean targets should be available, would make the claims more convincing.

Reproducibility is incomplete at submission time: the paper says code and models will be released, but many implementation details are deferred to an appendix that is not present in the provided manuscript.

The writing is understandable but often grammatically rough, with notation and equation descriptions that are sometimes imprecise. This does not invalidate the work, but it makes parts of the method harder to verify carefully.

strengths: Addresses a timely and practical problem: feed-forward/generalizable 3D Gaussian reconstruction in the presence of transient distractors during both training and inference. The problem setting is well motivated and distinct from scene-specific distractor-free NeRF/3DGS methods.

The proposed framework has a coherent design: reference-based mask prediction exploits multi-view consistency, mask refinement reduces over-masking, and the inference stage adds reference scoring plus Gaussian pruning. The components are reasonably connected to the stated failure modes.

Empirical results show consistent improvements over MVSplat/Pixelsplat baselines and several adapted distractor-free masking methods on RobustNeRF and On-the-go scenes, with meaningful gains in PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS.

The paper includes useful ablations for mask prediction, refinement, auxiliary loss, reference scoring, pruning, segmentation model choice, and reference/pool size, which supports the main architectural choices.
The work recognizes limitations, especially common occlusions and efficiency overhead, and includes qualitative failure cases.
weaknesses: The real-data evaluation is fairly small and somewhat specialized: training uses On-the-go scenes and testing uses two held-out On-the-go scenes plus RobustNeRF. This is useful, but still limited evidence for broad real-world generalization.

The evaluation protocol for inference is not fully convincing. Candidate reference pools are constructed from views closest to the query and may include cleaner images; this is plausible for analysis but can make the reference scoring setting easier than unconstrained capture. The practical setting is discussed but not rigorously evaluated.

The claimed superiority of the predicted distractor masks is mostly qualitative. Given the paper emphasizes mask prediction and even claims performance beyond scene-specific methods, quantitative mask metrics or human/annotated evaluation would substantially strengthen the claim.

Baselines based on scene-specific distractor methods are adapted into the generalizable training loss, but these adaptations may not be optimal or fully faithful to the original methods. This weakens conclusions that DGGS is superior to those approaches rather than superior to these particular integrations.

Synthetic distractor construction uses pasted COCO objects and may not model true 3D-consistent transient geometry, lighting, occlusion, or motion. It is a useful stress test but not strong evidence by itself.
Experiments are at low resolution, and the method depends on precomputed segmentation and two-stage inference; the efficiency and scalability story is only partially addressed.

Clarity and writing are uneven, with grammar issues, overloaded notation, and some confusing descriptions of mask fusion/decoupling. Reproducibility is also incomplete because code is only promised upon publication.

strengths: The paper targets a practical and timely problem: making feed-forward/generalizable 3D Gaussian Splatting robust to transient distractors during both training and inference.

The proposed framework is coherent and modular, combining reference-based mask prediction, mask refinement, reference scoring, and distractor pruning in a way that can plausibly be integrated into existing generalizable 3DGS pipelines.

The paper includes a reasonable set of ablations showing that the reference-based mask prediction is the main contributor, with additional gains from mask refinement, auxiliary loss, reference scoring, and pruning.

The authors evaluate on both real distractor datasets and a constructed synthetic distractor benchmark, and they compare against several adapted generalizable 3DGS and distractor-free reconstruction methods.
Qualitative results and mask visualizations are helpful for understanding the intended behavior of the method and its failure modes.
weaknesses: The novelty is somewhat incremental despite the new task framing. Much of the method is a combination of residual/robust masking, semantic segmentation priors, multi-view warping, reference selection, and primitive pruning, all of which are close to existing ideas in robust NeRF/3DGS and distractor-free reconstruction.

The real-data evaluation is limited. The main quantitative mean is over five RobustNeRF scenes, with additional On-the-go quantitative results only for DGGS-TR because the evaluation views still contain distractors. This weakens support for the broader claim of robust in-the-wild generalizable reconstruction.

The inference evaluation protocol may favor the proposed method: the scene-image pool is built from views closest to the query and is said to include both distractor-containing and few distractor-free data. This raises concerns about how realistic the protocol is and how much the gains depend on access to unusually favorable nearby clean references.

Baseline comparisons are not fully convincing. Scene-specific distractor-free methods are adapted into Mvsplat in simplified ways, and at least one important component of NeRF-HuGS is excluded as impractical. These adaptations may not represent the strongest possible competing systems.

The synthetic benchmark is not sufficiently validated. Distractors are pasted from COCO with random placement, scaling, and rotation, which may not capture realistic geometry, lighting, occlusion, motion, or view-consistent transient behavior; improvements there may not transfer to real capture conditions.

The paper uses very low image resolution, 192x256, for all experiments. It is unclear whether the method remains effective and efficient at practically relevant resolutions, especially given the additional segmentation, two-stage inference, and pruning machinery.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The exact training/inference code is promised only upon publication, and several important implementation details are under-specified, including mask thresholds, entity filling rules, candidate-pool construction, segmentation preprocessing, and details of the modified rasterization/warping pipeline.

The paper’s claims are stronger than the evidence. In particular, statements about outperforming scene-specific distractor-free methods and laying a foundation for the task are not fully supported by the limited, somewhat asymmetric comparisons and narrow evaluation setting.

Presentation quality is below top-tier standards in places, with grammatical issues, inconsistent terminology, and some equations/descriptions that are difficult to parse. This makes the technical contribution harder to assess than necessary.

strengths: The paper identifies a timely and practically important gap: existing generalizable 3DGS methods are vulnerable to transient distractors during both training and inference, while most distractor-free reconstruction methods are scene-specific and optimization-based.

The proposed DGGS framework is conceptually coherent: reference-based mask prediction, mask refinement, inference-time reference scoring, and distractor pruning all address distinct failure modes of feed-forward 3DGS under distractors.

The empirical results are broadly convincing within the proposed setting, with consistent gains over MVSplat/Pixelsplat and several adapted distractor-free baselines on RobustNeRF, On-the-go scenes, and synthetic distractor data.

The ablation studies are useful and fairly extensive, isolating the effects of reference-based masking, mask refinement, auxiliary loss, reference scoring, pruning, segmentation choices, mask fusion, and reference count.
The paper is well motivated and includes helpful qualitative evidence showing reduced artifacts and improved mask prediction, which is important for this visually driven problem.
weaknesses: The evaluation remains somewhat narrow for the strength of the claims: training uses a limited set of distractor scenes, and the main quantitative evaluation is concentrated on a small number of benchmarks at low image resolution.

The baseline comparisons are partly based on adaptations of scene-specific distractor-free methods into the MVSplat training loss. These adaptations may not represent the strongest possible versions of those methods, and the paper could better justify fairness and implementation fidelity.

The inference setup assumes access to a candidate image pool near the target view and benefits from reference re-selection; the practical constraints and sensitivity to pool quality, camera coverage, and absence of clean-ish views are not fully characterized.
Some claims about mask superiority over scene-specific methods are supported mainly by qualitative examples rather than rigorous mask metrics against ground-truth distractor annotations.

The method still relies on accurate poses, geometry-based warping, rendered depth, and sometimes pretrained segmentation; robustness to pose noise, calibration errors, and more unconstrained captures is not sufficiently studied.

Reproducibility details are incomplete: the paper describes many components and hyperparameters, but implementation specifics for baseline integration, segmentation caching, pruning thresholds, and training data construction would need to be clearer for reliable reproduction.
